front: What is the difference between Sunni and Shi'a Muslims?
p1: Islam has around 1.5 billion followers → Sunni Muslims (85-90%) believe Abu Bakr, who was not from Muhammad's family, was a rightly guided leader after Muhammad.
p2: Shi'a Muslims (10-15%) believe leaders should be Muhammad's family and descendants → they see Ali as the first leader and call leaders Imams.
p3: Sunni leaders are called Khalifahs (caliphs) → Sunnis see four 'rightly guided' Khalifahs: Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman and Ali.
s: Islam has around 1.5 billion followers → Sunni Muslims (85-90%) believe Abu Bakr, who was not from Muhammad's family, was a rightly guided leader after Muhammad.
Shi'a Muslims (10-15%) believe leaders should be Muhammad's family and descendants → they see Ali as the first leader and call leaders Imams.
Sunni leaders are called Khalifahs (caliphs) → Sunnis see four 'rightly guided' Khalifahs: Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman and Ali.

front: What are the Six Beliefs of Sunni Islam and where do they come from?
p1: Six Beliefs: Allah (Tawhid), angels (Malaikah), books (Kutub), messengers (Risalah), the Last Day (Akhirah) and the decree of Allah (Qadr).
p2: They come from the Qur'an and the Hadith → a Hadith in Sahih Muslim (Kitab al-Iman) tells how Jibril, disguised as a man, asked Muhammad about faith.
p3: Muhammad answered by listing the beliefs, then told Umar the questioner was Gabriel → 'He came to teach you your religion.'
s: Six Beliefs: Allah (Tawhid), angels (Malaikah), books (Kutub), messengers (Risalah), the Last Day (Akhirah) and the decree of Allah (Qadr).
They come from the Qur'an and the Hadith → a Hadith in Sahih Muslim (Kitab al-Iman) tells how Jibril, disguised as a man, asked Muhammad about faith.
Muhammad answered by listing the beliefs, then told Umar the questioner was Gabriel → 'He came to teach you your religion.'

front: How do the Six Beliefs affect Muslims' lives?
p1: Allah: Muslims worship and thank him in prayers → angels: after prayers they turn their heads left and right and say 'peace be upon you' to the malaikah.
p2: Books: many study the Qur'an at home or in mosque schools → messengers: Muslims are often named after prophets and use their stories as guidance.
p3: Day of Judgement: Muslims live as Allah guides, to be judged well → funerals speak of it; decree: Muslims try to accept Allah's will.
s: Allah: Muslims worship and thank him in prayers → angels: after prayers they turn their heads left and right and say 'peace be upon you' to the malaikah.
Books: many study the Qur'an at home or in mosque schools → messengers: Muslims are often named after prophets and use their stories as guidance.
Day of Judgement: Muslims live as Allah guides, to be judged well → funerals speak of it; decree: Muslims try to accept Allah's will.

front: What are the Five Roots of Shi'a Islam?
p1: Usul ad-Din (the Five Roots): the central Shi'a beliefs, from the Qur'an, the Hadith and the early Imams → a root holds something up, so it is a metaphor.
p2: Tawhid: one God, who cannot be split into parts → Nubuwwah: belief in the prophets from Adam to Muhammad, as guides and role models.
p3: Adl: Allah is fair and just and will make everything fair in the end → Shi'a Muslims aim to be just in their own lives.
s: Usul ad-Din (the Five Roots): the central Shi'a beliefs, from the Qur'an, the Hadith and the early Imams → a root holds something up, so it is a metaphor.
Tawhid: one God, who cannot be split into parts → Nubuwwah: belief in the prophets from Adam to Muhammad, as guides and role models.
Adl: Allah is fair and just and will make everything fair in the end → Shi'a Muslims aim to be just in their own lives.

front: What are Imamah and Mi'ad, and how do Shi'a groups differ?
p1: Imamah: Allah chose leaders of the Muslim community → Shi'a believe Muhammad, his daughter Fatimah and a line of Imams starting with Ali were chosen; they are seen as perfect, pure and always correct.
p2: Disagreement: Twelver Shi'a are the majority → Sevener Shi'a differ on who the true Imams are.
p3: Mi'ad: belief in the Day of Judgement and resurrection to an afterlife that lasts forever → people are judged on their actions, to go to Jannah or Jahannam.
s: Imamah: Allah chose leaders of the Muslim community → Shi'a believe Muhammad, his daughter Fatimah and a line of Imams starting with Ali were chosen; they are seen as perfect, pure and always correct.
Disagreement: Twelver Shi'a are the majority → Sevener Shi'a differ on who the true Imams are.
Mi'ad: belief in the Day of Judgement and resurrection to an afterlife that lasts forever → people are judged on their actions, to go to Jannah or Jahannam.

front: What does Tawhid mean?
p1: Tawhid: there is one God and God is one being → nothing in the universe is as supreme as God, and God should not be understood as a Trinity.
p2: Muslims cannot picture Allah, who is not a physical being → it is forbidden to draw Allah; more than 100 names or descriptions are found in the Qur'an and Hadith.
p3: Shirk: putting something on a level with Allah, or worshipping anything else → seen as the worst sin in Islam.
s: Tawhid: there is one God and God is one being → nothing in the universe is as supreme as God, and God should not be understood as a Trinity.
Muslims cannot picture Allah, who is not a physical being → it is forbidden to draw Allah; more than 100 names or descriptions are found in the Qur'an and Hadith.
Shirk: putting something on a level with Allah, or worshipping anything else → seen as the worst sin in Islam.

front: What do transcendence, immanence, omnipotence and beneficence mean?
p1: Transcendence: Allah is outside and beyond the universe he created → immanence: Allah acts in the universe; 'closer to him than his jugular vein'.
p2: Omnipotence: Allah is all-powerful and can do anything, creating everything from nothing → 'power over all things'.
p3: Beneficence: Allah is loving, kind and generous towards his creation → 'your Lord's bounty is not restricted'.
s: Transcendence: Allah is outside and beyond the universe he created → immanence: Allah acts in the universe; 'closer to him than his jugular vein'.
Omnipotence: Allah is all-powerful and can do anything, creating everything from nothing → 'power over all things'.
Beneficence: Allah is loving, kind and generous towards his creation → 'your Lord's bounty is not restricted'.

front: What do mercy and justice show about Allah, and why does his nature matter?
p1: Mercy: 113 of the Qur'an's 114 Surahs begin 'In the name of God, the Lord of Mercy' → some Muslims believe Jahannam is not forever, which shows Allah's mercy.
p2: Justice (Adl in Shi'a Islam): Allah treats people fairly by how they chose to live → he expects people to treat others fairly.
p3: Thinking about Allah's nature brings comfort, shows why to worship him and brings Muslims closer to him.
s: Mercy: 113 of the Qur'an's 114 Surahs begin 'In the name of God, the Lord of Mercy' → some Muslims believe Jahannam is not forever, which shows Allah's mercy.
Justice (Adl in Shi'a Islam): Allah treats people fairly by how they chose to live → he expects people to treat others fairly.
Thinking about Allah's nature brings comfort, shows why to worship him and brings Muslims closer to him.

front: Why is Risalah important for Muslims?
p1: Risalah (Nubuwwah in Shi'a): belief in the prophets, messengers chosen by Allah to teach the right way to live → Muhammad said there were 124,000 and Muslims believe in all of them.
p2: Prophets give guidance and are role models → many Muslims are named after them.
p3: It shows links with Christianity and Judaism → it is one of the Six Beliefs for Sunnis and one of the Five Roots for Shi'a.
s: Risalah (Nubuwwah in Shi'a): belief in the prophets, messengers chosen by Allah to teach the right way to live → Muhammad said there were 124,000 and Muslims believe in all of them.
Prophets give guidance and are role models → many Muslims are named after them.
It shows links with Christianity and Judaism → it is one of the Six Beliefs for Sunnis and one of the Five Roots for Shi'a.

front: What do the lives of Adam, Ibrahim and Isma'il teach Muslims?
p1: Adam: the first prophet and man, who lived with Hawwa (Eve) in a garden → tempted by Iblis, a fallen angel, they were sent out.
p2: Ibrahim: 'Allah's friend', an example of faith → rebuilt the Ka'bah with Isma'il, believed the first religious building to Allah on earth.
p3: Ibrahim dreamed Allah asked him to sacrifice Isma'il, who freely offered → Allah stopped him and praised both; Muslims see this as trusting Allah.
s: Adam: the first prophet and man, who lived with Hawwa (Eve) in a garden → tempted by Iblis, a fallen angel, they were sent out.
Ibrahim: 'Allah's friend', an example of faith → rebuilt the Ka'bah with Isma'il, believed the first religious building to Allah on earth.

front: What do the lives of Musa, Dawud and Isa teach Muslims?
p1: Musa (Moses): chosen to free the Israelites from slavery in Egypt → his life inspires Muslims that Allah rewards effort and good wins over evil.
p2: Dawud (David): remembered for wisdom, prayers and victory over Goliath → shows Allah blesses his chosen ones; given the Zabur.
p3: Isa (Jesus): a prophet only, not God, and not killed on a cross → Allah saved him; he did miracles and was given the Injil.
s: Musa (Moses): chosen to free the Israelites from slavery in Egypt → his life inspires Muslims that Allah rewards effort and good wins over evil.
Dawud (David): remembered for wisdom, prayers and victory over Goliath → shows Allah blesses his chosen ones; given the Zabur.
Isa (Jesus): a prophet only, not God, and not killed on a cross → Allah saved him; he did miracles and was given the Injil.

front: Why is Muhammad the most important prophet?
p1: Muhammad is the final prophet, the 'seal of the prophets' (Surah 33:40) → the line of prophets was sealed after him, and he had the great qualities of all the prophets before him.
p2: His message is for all people at all times → other messages were for particular people at particular times.
p3: The Qur'an calls him a 'light' and 'an excellent model' → following the Qur'an and his example (Sunnah and Hadith) is following Allah's wishes.
s: Muhammad is the final prophet, the 'seal of the prophets' (Surah 33:40) → the line of prophets was sealed after him, and he had the great qualities of all the prophets before him.

The Qur'an calls him a 'light' and 'an excellent model' → following the Qur'an and his example (Sunnah and Hadith) is following Allah's wishes.

front: What are the Muslim holy books (Kutubullah)?
p1: Kutubullah: 'books of Allah' from prophets → only the Qur'an has the complete and correct guidance; Muslims believe some of Allah's message was mistaken or lost in other books, but respect them.
p2: Sahifah: scrolls of Ibrahim and Musa, believed lost → Tawrat: scriptures of Musa, revealed just for the Jewish people at a particular time.
p3: Zabur: the 150 Psalms given to Dawud → Injil: the original gospel given to Isa, lost, forgotten or altered; the four gospels contain some of it.
s: Kutubullah: 'books of Allah' from prophets → only the Qur'an has the complete and correct guidance; Muslims believe some of Allah's message was mistaken or lost in other books, but respect them.
Sahifah: scrolls of Ibrahim and Musa, believed lost → Tawrat: scriptures of Musa, revealed just for the Jewish people at a particular time.
Zabur: the 150 Psalms given to Dawud → Injil: the original gospel given to Isa, lost, forgotten or altered; the four gospels contain some of it.

front: What do Muslims believe about the Qur'an?
p1: The Qur'an was revealed to Muhammad as the final and complete message for all people → Jibril spoke it to him over 1400 years ago, and the text has not changed.
p2: It says of itself 'Let there be no doubt about it, it is from the Lord of the Worlds' → and that it is 'free from any distortion'.
p3: The Qur'an has 114 Surahs → Muslims look to it, and the other books, to understand how to live.

front: Why are the holy books important to Muslims today?
p1: Earlier books record Allah's messages through the prophets → some (Tawrat) are for particular times and peoples, and others (Injil) were lost or changed.
p2: All the holy books point towards the final message given in the Qur'an.
p3: Muslims seek to understand how to live by looking in the holy books, especially the Qur'an → Muslims differ in how important they see them in their lives.

All the holy books point towards the final message given in the Qur'an.

front: What are malaikah like and why do they matter?
p1: Malaikah (angels) are created by Allah to help govern the universe and the laws of nature → they have no free will and do exactly what Allah tells them.
p2: Belief in malaikah is one of the Six Beliefs for Sunnis → they help Muslims in need, and each person has two recording their deeds.
p3: The angel on the right shoulder records good deeds and the one on the left bad → these are presented to Allah on the Day of Judgement.

Belief in malaikah is one of the Six Beliefs for Sunnis → they help Muslims in need, and each person has two recording their deeds.
The angel on the right shoulder records good deeds and the one on the left bad → these are presented to Allah on the Day of Judgement.

front: What are the roles of Jibril, Izra'il and Mika'il?
p1: Jibril (Gabriel): communicates Allah's messages to his prophets → delivered the whole Qur'an to Muhammad over 23 years, appearing as an ordinary human.
p2: Izra'il (Azrael): the angel of death, who takes each person's soul at death → as instructed by Allah, returning it to him.
p3: Mika'il (Michael): maintains life on earth → in charge of plants and rain and other natural processes.
s: Jibril (Gabriel): communicates Allah's messages to his prophets → delivered the whole Qur'an to Muhammad over 23 years, appearing as an ordinary human.
Izra'il (Azrael): the angel of death, who takes each person's soul at death → as instructed by Allah, returning it to him.
Mika'il (Michael): maintains life on earth → in charge of plants and rain and other natural processes.

front: What is Al-Qadr and why does it matter?
p1: Al-Qadr (predestination): Allah has decided certain things that will happen and put fixed laws in place → 'He regulates all things'; it includes genes and the situation people are born into.
p2: It shows Allah's power and knowledge, and that the laws of the universe are for the good of people.
p3: Muslims are comforted that everything happens for a reason in Allah's plan → it is one of the Six Beliefs of Sunni Muslims.
s: Al-Qadr (predestination): Allah has decided certain things that will happen and put fixed laws in place → 'He regulates all things'; it includes genes and the situation people are born into.
It shows Allah's power and knowledge, and that the laws of the universe are for the good of people.
Muslims are comforted that everything happens for a reason in Allah's plan → it is one of the Six Beliefs of Sunni Muslims.

front: How do Al-Qadr, human freedom and the Day of Judgement fit together?
p1: Humans can choose good or evil (apart from genes and social situation) → 'let those who wish to believe in it do so'.
p2: Prophets will always succeed, as part of Allah's plan → but people choose whether to believe; prayer can change what Allah does if it does not conflict with his plans.
p3: Allah will not condemn people for how they were born → he judges them on the choices they were free to make.
s: Humans can choose good or evil (apart from genes and social situation) → 'let those who wish to believe in it do so'.
Prophets will always succeed, as part of Allah's plan → but people choose whether to believe; prayer can change what Allah does if it does not conflict with his plans.
Allah will not condemn people for how they were born → he judges them on the choices they were free to make.

front: What is Akhirah, and what happens at the Day of Judgement?
p1: Akhirah: life after death → everyone will die and be raised to life again by the One who created them the first time.
p2: At death Izra'il takes the soul to wait for the Day of Judgement → on that day the dead are resurrected and judged on their choices, recorded by the angels.
p3: Those who followed Allah's guidance go to Jannah (paradise) → those who did not go to Jahannam (hell).

front: What do the Qur'an and Muslims say about Jannah, Jahannam and different views of Akhirah?
p1: Jannah: a comfortable, pleasant place, with Gardens of lasting bliss → Jahannam: a place of pain and suffering, where the Fire will scorch faces.
p2: Some Muslims see these images as symbolic → others think they will be exactly as the Qur'an describes.
p3: Some believe resurrection will be physical, so Muslims are buried not cremated → many think Jahannam is forever, others that it is not, because Allah is most merciful.

Some Muslims see these images as symbolic → others think they will be exactly as the Qur'an describes.

front: Why is marriage (nikah) important for Muslims?
p1: Nikah is a contract between two people to spend their lives together → it follows the Sunnah of Muhammad, who married: 'Marriage is my Sunnah'.
p2: It encourages love and companionship → it treats sex as valuable, so discourages casual sex.
p3: It gives a structure for having and raising children together → it is an important part of society, bringing families and friends together.
s: Nikah is a contract between two people to spend their lives together → it follows the Sunnah of Muhammad, who married: 'Marriage is my Sunnah'.
It encourages love and companionship → it treats sex as valuable, so discourages casual sex.

front: What happens at a nikah ceremony, and what are the Muslim teachings on marriage?
p1: The bride gives her consent, often represented by a male guardian → the groom proposes and gives the agreed mahr (payment).
p2: Marriage should be a free choice → many are arranged, but forcing marriage is against Islam (Surah 4:19).
p3: A man can have up to four wives only if he treats them equally → most have one; couples should stay faithful.
s: The bride gives her consent, often represented by a male guardian → the groom proposes and gives the agreed mahr (payment).
Marriage should be a free choice → many are arranged, but forcing marriage is against Islam (Surah 4:19).
A man can have up to four wives only if he treats them equally → most have one; couples should stay faithful.

front: What do non-religious people think about living together unmarried, and how do Muslims reply?
p1: For marriage: financial and emotional structure, a commitment to stay faithful → a chance to tell everyone they will stay together for life.
p2: Against: it is not needed to show love → around 40% of UK marriages end in divorce, and weddings can be expensive (over £25,000 on average).
p3: Muslims are against cohabitation and support nikah → it makes people more serious, is better for children, and keeps sex within marriage.
s: For marriage: financial and emotional structure, a commitment to stay faithful → a chance to tell everyone they will stay together for life.

Muslims are against cohabitation and support nikah → it makes people more serious, is better for children, and keeps sex within marriage.

front: What do Muslims teach about sex and relationships outside marriage?
p1: Islam accepts sex as an expression of love and for procreation → but it should only happen within nikah.
p2: Premarital sex is a serious sin against Allah → Muslims are taught to 'guard their chastity'; Muhammad taught that if a man and woman are alone, Satan joins them.
p3: Adultery is 'an outrage, and an evil path' (Surah 17:32) → the Qur'an gives serious punishments, though many believe Allah forgives the truly sorry.
s: Islam accepts sex as an expression of love and for procreation → but it should only happen within nikah.
Premarital sex is a serious sin against Allah → Muslims are taught to 'guard their chastity'; Muhammad taught that if a man and woman are alone, Satan joins them.
Adultery is 'an outrage, and an evil path' (Surah 17:32) → the Qur'an gives serious punishments, though many believe Allah forgives the truly sorry.

front: What do Muslims teach about homosexuality?
p1: The Qur'an teaches that homosexuality is a sin → Muslims who see it as wrong say the purpose of sex is reproduction, which same-sex sex cannot achieve.
p2: The story of Lot: he is angry with men lusting after men → Allah destroys the region, apart from Lot and his followers (Surah 7:80-84).
p3: In many Muslim countries it is illegal → in some, such as Indonesia and Turkey, it is not, but same-sex marriage is not allowed; some gay Muslims support LGBT rights within Islam.

The story of Lot: he is angry with men lusting after men → Allah destroys the region, apart from Lot and his followers (Surah 7:80-84).
In many Muslim countries it is illegal → in some, such as Indonesia and Turkey, it is not, but same-sex marriage is not allowed; some gay Muslims support LGBT rights within Islam.

front: What do non-religious people think about sexual relationships, and how do Muslims reply?
p1: Humanists and atheists say people should choose freely but responsibly → premarital sex shows compatibility, and contraception limits STDs and pregnancy.
p2: Homosexuality is natural, and same-sex marriage is legal in the UK → most see adultery as wrong, but not a crime.
p3: Muslims reply that sex is only permitted by Allah within marriage → so see these views as leading people away from Allah's guidance.

Homosexuality is natural, and same-sex marriage is legal in the UK → most see adultery as wrong, but not a crime.

front: Why is the family important in Islam, and how should families treat each other?
p1: The family is at the heart of the Muslim community → it gives children a secure childhood to be raised as Muslims.
p2: Muhammad was married and had children → Muslims follow his example in having families and in how they treat them; each person has particular roles.
p3: Muslims must respect parents, especially mothers (Surah 46:15) → Muhammad said 'The best of you is the one who behaves best towards the members of his family'.
s: The family is at the heart of the Muslim community → it gives children a secure childhood to be raised as Muslims.
Muhammad was married and had children → Muslims follow his example in having families and in how they treat them; each person has particular roles.
Muslims must respect parents, especially mothers (Surah 46:15) → Muhammad said 'The best of you is the one who behaves best towards the members of his family'.

front: How do families strengthen the Muslim community, and what do Muslims think of different family types?
p1: The ummah is the worldwide Muslim community → families strengthen it by raising children as good Muslims, teaching them and sending them to madrasah.
p2: Muslims strive for the nuclear family, as Muhammad lived and the Qur'an describes → many also care for extended family, especially elderly parents.
p3: Muslims prefer blended families to single-parent families, and do not support same-sex parenting → they believe Allah made men and women for heterosexual relationships.

front: How does the Muslim community support families?
p1: Worship at the mosque, where Muslims meet and are guided → books and classes on Islam for young and old.
p2: Birth rites: the adhan is said into a baby's ear; around day seven the aqiqah → the head is shaved, hair weight in gold or silver given to charity, and a feast.
p3: Death rites: prayers, the body washed and wrapped in white shrouds, buried without a coffin facing Makkah → counselling from mosque leaders and shari'ah councils.

front: Why does the mosque's support matter to Muslim families?
p1: The Qur'an teaches Muslims to work as a community → 'Hold fast to God's rope all together' (Surah 3:103).
p2: It helps families bring up children as Muslims → information, classes and rites of passage.
p3: Counselling by respected leaders helps solve problems → and in Britain, where Muslims can feel stereotyped, communities give a sense of belonging and acceptance.

front: Why are many Muslims against contraception?
p1: Few direct teachings exist → thinkers use general ideas; children are a blessing and raising families is an important duty.
p2: Contraception gets in the way of Allah's plans → 'Allah grants children to whoever He wills' (Surah 42:49).
p3: Allah will provide, so not having children for fear of cost is wrong → 'Do not kill your children for fear of poverty' (Surah 17:31).

Contraception gets in the way of Allah's plans → 'Allah grants children to whoever He wills' (Surah 42:49).

front: Why do some Muslims support contraception?
p1: Some accept it within marriage → Surah 2 says no mother should be burdened beyond what she can bear, read as allowing a two-year gap.
p2: Asked about coitus interruptus, Muhammad said 'It is better for you not to do it' → he did not forbid it, so some say modern forms are not forbidden.
p3: Many support it if a woman's health is at risk or a child would inherit a terrible illness → permanent forms such as sterilisation are generally forbidden.

front: What do non-religious people and situation ethics say about contraception, and how do Muslims reply?
p1: Humanists and atheists do not follow the Qur'an → contraception lets couples express love without children, choose when to have children and prevent STDs.
p2: Situation ethics: do the most loving thing → often that is using contraception, so families can plan.
p3: Muslims reply that children are a blessing and Allah will provide → they would not approve of choosing no children, and worry about a rise in casual sex.

front: Why do Muslims see divorce as bad, and why do most accept it?
p1: Marriage is important, and divorce can harm children → Muhammad said 'Of all the things Allah has made lawful He hates divorce the most' (Abu Dawud).
p2: Most Muslims accept divorce because Allah has made it lawful → there is a clear procedure in the Qur'an.
p3: Marriage is a contract → if it is broken, it can be cancelled; the Qur'an prefers mending relationships if possible.
s: Marriage is important, and divorce can harm children → Muhammad said 'Of all the things Allah has made lawful He hates divorce the most' (Abu Dawud).
Most Muslims accept divorce because Allah has made it lawful → there is a clear procedure in the Qur'an.

front: What are the stages of divorce in Islam, and how does Shi'a Islam differ?

Salvation: being saved from sin → people are lost from their relationship with God and in danger of Hell, so need saving.
Atonement: healing the relationship between humans and God → being 'at one' with God.

front: How does Jesus bring salvation, and what are grace and repentance?
p1: Jesus' death paid for people's sins against God's laws → God the Father sends the Son to die; people get a chance to be saved but must still try to have a good relationship with God.
p2: Grace: the love of God → offered whether people deserve it or not.
p3: Repentance: being sorry for bad things you have done → doing your best not to do them again.
s: Jesus' death paid for people's sins against God's laws → God the Father sends the Son to die; people get a chance to be saved but must still try to have a good relationship with God.
Grace: the love of God → offered whether people deserve it or not.
Repentance: being sorry for bad things you have done → doing your best not to do them again.

front: How do Christians disagree about getting salvation, and why does it matter?
p1: Roman Catholic, Orthodox and some Church of England Christians: atonement through the sacraments of baptism, confirmation, confession and the Eucharist → and a good Christian life.
p2: Many Protestants: the most important thing is accepting Jesus as their Lord and Saviour.
p3: It matters because Adam and Eve's sin and people's own sins separate them from God → salvation gives a chance of a good relationship with God, Heaven and eternal life.
s: Roman Catholic, Orthodox and some Church of England Christians: atonement through the sacraments of baptism, confirmation, confession and the Eucharist → and a good Christian life.
Many Protestants: the most important thing is accepting Jesus as their Lord and Saviour.
It matters because Adam and Eve's sin and people's own sins separate them from God → salvation gives a chance of a good relationship with God, Heaven and eternal life.

front: What are the two main Christian views about life after death?
p1: Eschatology: beliefs about death and life after death. Resurrection of the body (some Protestants): the dead stay in the grave until the Last Day, after the Second Coming → then all get new 'resurrection' bodies; evidence: the empty tomb.
p2: Immortality of the soul (many Christians): the immortal, not-physical soul goes to Heaven at death, leaving the body behind → evidence: Jesus tells the robber 'paradise that day', and Moses and Elijah speak from Heaven.
s: Eschatology: beliefs about death and life after death. Resurrection of the body (some Protestants): the dead stay in the grave until the Last Day, after the Second Coming → then all get new 'resurrection' bodies; evidence: the empty tomb.

Immortality of the soul (many Christians): the immortal, not-physical soul goes to Heaven at death, leaving the body behind → evidence: Jesus tells the robber 'paradise that day', and Moses and Elijah speak from Heaven.

front: What do Christians believe about the Final Judgement and why does it matter?
p1: God will judge everyone → this decides the afterlife; Protestants say it depends on faith in Jesus, Roman Catholics on choices made in life.
p2: Sheep and Goats (Matthew 25:31-46): judged on whether people helped those in need → 2 Corinthians 5:1-10: judged on good and bad deeds.
p3: So Christians try to live as God wants and seek forgiveness → Heaven and Hell give life a larger purpose.
s: God will judge everyone → this decides the afterlife; Protestants say it depends on faith in Jesus, Roman Catholics on choices made in life.
Sheep and Goats (Matthew 25:31-46): judged on whether people helped those in need → 2 Corinthians 5:1-10: judged on good and bad deeds.
So Christians try to live as God wants and seek forgiveness → Heaven and Hell give life a larger purpose.

front: What are moral and natural evil, and what is the problem of evil?
p1: Moral evil: suffering caused by human choices, such as war → the same as sin; natural evil: suffering from natural processes, such as floods.
p2: God is omnipotent, benevolent and omniscient → each seems to clash with evil: why allow it, or create a world knowing it would happen?
p3: There should be no evil, but there is → so either God lacks one of these qualities, or God does not exist.
s: Moral evil: suffering caused by human choices, such as war → the same as sin; natural evil: suffering from natural processes, such as floods.
God is omnipotent, benevolent and omniscient → each seems to clash with evil: why allow it, or create a world knowing it would happen?
There should be no evil, but there is → so either God lacks one of these qualities, or God does not exist.

front: What biblical responses do Christians give to the problem of evil?
p1: Job: a sinless man whom God allows Satan to make suffer; Job meets God and decides humans have no right to question him → trust that God knows best; but how far should this trust go?
p2: Psalms: good, religious people suffer too, and suffering can help people understand God → but why would God make suffering needed for this?
s: Job: a sinless man whom God allows Satan to make suffer; Job meets God and decides humans have no right to question him → trust that God knows best; but how far should this trust go?
Psalms: good, religious people suffer too, and suffering can help people understand God → but why would God make suffering needed for this?

front: What theoretical responses do Christians give to the problem of evil?
p1: Free will: God made people free to have a real relationship with him and choose his laws → so they can choose evil, as Adam and Eve did; but is all the suffering worth it?
p2: Vale of soul-making (St Irenaeus and John Hick): suffering is needed to learn to be good → the world is a 'vale' where we perfect our souls for Heaven; but why not create perfect souls?
s: Free will: God made people free to have a real relationship with him and choose his laws → so they can choose evil, as Adam and Eve did; but is all the suffering worth it?
Vale of soul-making (St Irenaeus and John Hick): suffering is needed to learn to be good → the world is a 'vale' where we perfect our souls for Heaven; but why not create perfect souls?

front: What does the Nicene Creed say about God, and why do Christians say God is one?
p1: Nicene Creed: one God, the Father almighty, maker of heaven and earth → the Son is 'eternally begotten of the Father, God from God… of one Being with the Father'.
p2: It calls the Holy Spirit 'the Lord, the giver of life' → worshipped and glorified with the Father and the Son.
p3: Christians are monotheist → Jesus says the 'Lord is one' (Mark 12:29); Roman Catholic and Church of England teaching agree.
s: Nicene Creed: one God, the Father almighty, maker of heaven and earth → the Son is 'eternally begotten of the Father, God from God… of one Being with the Father'.
It calls the Holy Spirit 'the Lord, the giver of life' → worshipped and glorified with the Father and the Son.
Christians are monotheist → Jesus says the 'Lord is one' (Mark 12:29); Roman Catholic and Church of England teaching agree.

front: What is justice and why does it matter to Christians?
p1: Justice: doing what is right and fair based on the law → laws are the rules of a country, meant to apply to everyone fairly.
p2: God is just and wants people to act with justice → the Ten Commandments, and Micah: 'Do what is right, love kindness, and walk humbly with God'.
p3: God is the final judge: 'Each person was judged according to what they had done' → Jesus added mercy and forgiveness.
s: Justice: doing what is right and fair based on the law → laws are the rules of a country, meant to apply to everyone fairly.
God is just and wants people to act with justice → the Ten Commandments, and Micah: 'Do what is right, love kindness, and walk humbly with God'.
God is the final judge: 'Each person was judged according to what they had done' → Jesus added mercy and forgiveness.

front: Why is justice important for victims, and for non-religious people?
p1: Victims usually feel it is fair if the person who hurt them is punished → and are pleased they cannot hurt anyone else.
p2: Christians are taught to 'defend the oppressed' by standing up for victims → Christian victims should forgive, not seek revenge; God will judge everyone justly.
p3: Atheists and Humanists value justice to protect people, keep peace and order, and treat people as they deserve → because they want what is good for people, not because God does.
s: Victims usually feel it is fair if the person who hurt them is punished → and are pleased they cannot hurt anyone else.
Christians are taught to 'defend the oppressed' by standing up for victims → Christian victims should forgive, not seek revenge; God will judge everyone justly.
Atheists and Humanists value justice to protect people, keep peace and order, and treat people as they deserve → because they want what is good for people, not because God does.

front: What is crime and why do people commit it?
p1: Crime: an act that breaks a law → examples are theft, violence, damaging property, murder, sexual offences and drug offences.
p2: Laws protect people and their possessions, mean people do not live in fear of crime, and give a clear idea of how people are expected to act.
p3: Suggested causes: poverty, social environment, addiction, hate (prejudice about race, gender or sexuality) and mental illness.
s: Crime: an act that breaks a law → examples are theft, violence, damaging property, murder, sexual offences and drug offences.
Laws protect people and their possessions, mean people do not live in fear of crime, and give a clear idea of how people are expected to act.
Suggested causes: poverty, social environment, addiction, hate (prejudice about race, gender or sexuality) and mental illness.

front: What do Christians teach about crime, and what do they do about it?
p1: Romans: 'Let every person be subject to the governing authorities' → Christians support the justice system, as stopping crime is loving.
p2: John 8: a woman caught in adultery is brought to Jesus → 'Let any one of you who is without sin be the first to throw a stone at her'.
p3: Prison Fellowship: Christian volunteers write to prisoners and help them contact family → Street Pastors walk the streets at night to keep people safe.
s: Romans: 'Let every person be subject to the governing authorities' → Christians support the justice system, as stopping crime is loving.
John 8: a woman caught in adultery is brought to Jesus → 'Let any one of you who is without sin be the first to throw a stone at her'.
Prison Fellowship: Christian volunteers write to prisoners and help them contact family → Street Pastors walk the streets at night to keep people safe.

front: What do Christians teach about good, evil and suffering?
p1: Good means following what God wants → 'those who have done what is good will rise to live, and… evil will rise to be condemned'.
p2: Many Christians see evil as the bad use of free will → some believe the Devil exists and tempts people to do wrong.
p3: Suffering is there because people commit sins → people can learn from it and should help others who suffer, as in the Sheep and the Goats.
s: Good means following what God wants → 'those who have done what is good will rise to live, and… evil will rise to be condemned'.
Many Christians see evil as the bad use of free will → some believe the Devil exists and tempts people to do wrong.
Suffering is there because people commit sins → people can learn from it and should help others who suffer, as in the Sheep and the Goats.

front: How do non-religious people explain suffering, and how do Christians reply?
p1: Atheists and Humanists: suffering comes from how the world works and people's choices, with no higher power of justice → it can be meaningless; everyone should work to remove its causes.
p2: Some say religion causes suffering → rules stop people doing what makes them happy, high standards cause guilt, and religious groups argue or use war.
p3: Christian reply: God's grace (forgiveness) allows guilt-free lives → Christianity teaches love and forgiveness for all, so is against war and violence.
s: Atheists and Humanists: suffering comes from how the world works and people's choices, with no higher power of justice → it can be meaningless; everyone should work to remove its causes.
Some say religion causes suffering → rules stop people doing what makes them happy, high standards cause guilt, and religious groups argue or use war.
Christian reply: God's grace (forgiveness) allows guilt-free lives → Christianity teaches love and forgiveness for all, so is against war and violence.

front: What punishments are used, and how do Christians view punishment?
p1: UK punishments: prison (from weeks to a whole life), community orders (40 to 300 hours of work) and fines.
p2: Some Christians focus on kindness and forgiveness for criminals → others support punishment as justice, and as love for victims.
p3: Many Christians support punishment but also help criminals and do not look down on them.
s: UK punishments: prison (from weeks to a whole life), community orders (40 to 300 hours of work) and fines.
Some Christians focus on kindness and forgiveness for criminals → others support punishment as justice, and as love for victims.
Many Christians support punishment but also help criminals and do not look down on them.

front: What does the Bible teach about punishment?
p1: Anyone who sets aside God's laws and teaches others to do the same will be called least in the kingdom of heaven.
p2: Parable of the Watchful Servant (Luke 12:35-48): a servant who knows what his master wants but does not do it will be punished severely; one who does wrong without knowing will be punished less.
p3: Revenge is wrong, so turn the other cheek (Matthew 5:38-39) → and 'Do not judge, or you too will be judged' (Matthew 7:1-5).
s: Anyone who sets aside God's laws and teaches others to do the same will be called least in the kingdom of heaven.
Parable of the Watchful Servant (Luke 12:35-48): a servant who knows what his master wants but does not do it will be punished severely; one who does wrong without knowing will be punished less.
Revenge is wrong, so turn the other cheek (Matthew 5:38-39) → and 'Do not judge, or you too will be judged' (Matthew 7:1-5).

d: take an eye for an eye

front: What are protection and retribution, and do Christians support them?
p1: Protection: keeping people safe from criminals → Christians support it as loving; 'Defend… the poor and oppressed' (Psalm 82:3); if crime comes from poverty, it may also mean helping criminals change.
p2: Retribution: doing wrong to those who have done wrong → some Christians support it as acting justly, using 'an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth' (Leviticus); others think revenge is wrong.
s: Protection: keeping people safe from criminals → Christians support it as loving; 'Defend… the poor and oppressed' (Psalm 82:3); if crime comes from poverty, it may also mean helping criminals change.
Retribution: doing wrong to those who have done wrong → some Christians support it as acting justly, using 'an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth' (Leviticus); others think revenge is wrong.

front: What are deterrence and reformation, and do Christians support them?
p1: Deterrence: punishments people would not want to experience, to put them off crime → some Christians support it as care for likely victims; others worry it ignores the person punished.
p2: Reformation: changing the criminal so they stop crime → many Christians support it, as Jesus forgave criminals and said forgive 'seventy-seven times'.
p3: Galatians 6: people caught in sin should be restored gently → Elizabeth Fry: 'punishment is not for revenge, but to lessen crime and reform the criminal'.
s: Deterrence: punishments people would not want to experience, to put them off crime → some Christians support it as care for likely victims; others worry it ignores the person punished.
Reformation: changing the criminal so they stop crime → many Christians support it, as Jesus forgave criminals and said forgive 'seventy-seven times'.
Galatians 6: people caught in sin should be restored gently → Elizabeth Fry: 'punishment is not for revenge, but to lessen crime and reform the criminal'.

front: What is forgiveness, and why do Christians forgive?
p1: Forgiveness: the victim decides to stop feeling angry with the person who hurt them → it does not mean forgetting the crime or letting the criminal go free.
p2: Jesus died so all people could be forgiven by God if they repent → Christians try to forgive, to be as much like God as they can.
p3: Rehabilitation: helping criminals back to a law-abiding life → a second chance for them and good for the community; critics say taxpayers should not pay.
s: Forgiveness: the victim decides to stop feeling angry with the person who hurt them → it does not mean forgetting the crime or letting the criminal go free.
Jesus died so all people could be forgiven by God if they repent → Christians try to forgive, to be as much like God as they can.
Rehabilitation: helping criminals back to a law-abiding life → a second chance for them and good for the community; critics say taxpayers should not pay.

front: What is restorative justice, and why do Christians support it?
p1: Restorative justice: criminals meet their victims and hear about the hurt they caused → the victim understands more about the crime; the aim is to restore or mend the harm.
p2: Supporters say the criminal must take the hurt seriously → and is more likely to feel sorry and want to change.
p3: Jesus taught to make peace rather than go to court: 'go and make peace first' → Prison Fellowship's Sycamore Tree programme is one example.
s: Restorative justice: criminals meet their victims and hear about the hurt they caused → the victim understands more about the crime; the aim is to restore or mend the harm.
Supporters say the criminal must take the hurt seriously → and is more likely to feel sorry and want to change.
Jesus taught to make peace rather than go to court: 'go and make peace first' → Prison Fellowship's Sycamore Tree programme is one example.

front: How should Christians treat criminals?
p1: Laws are needed for an ordered and fair society (the Ten Commandments) → punishments should be fair: 'Speak up and judge fairly; defend the rights of the poor and needy'.
p2: Christians also show love and support to criminals → visiting prisoners (Sheep and the Goats), punishment that rehabilitates, and mercy: 'Blessed are the merciful, for they will be shown mercy'.
p3: Christians support human rights, out of love and respect for all → torture is against human rights and against teachings of love and support.
s: Laws are needed for an ordered and fair society (the Ten Commandments) → punishments should be fair: 'Speak up and judge fairly; defend the rights of the poor and needy'.
Christians also show love and support to criminals → visiting prisoners (Sheep and the Goats), punishment that rehabilitates, and mercy: 'Blessed are the merciful, for they will be shown mercy'.
Christians support human rights, out of love and respect for all → torture is against human rights and against teachings of love and support.

front: What is situation ethics, and what do Christians think about fair trials and juries?
p1: Situation ethics: the only rule is 'love your neighbour' → in each situation, do the most loving thing for everyone, including victim and criminal.
p2: It can mean breaking a Bible rule if that is most loving → so many Christians do not support it.
p3: Fair trial: Christians agree → trial by jury (citizens decide guilt) is seen as good because evidence is fully heard, so the accused is judged fairly.
s: Situation ethics: the only rule is 'love your neighbour' → in each situation, do the most loving thing for everyone, including victim and criminal.
It can mean breaking a Bible rule if that is most loving → so many Christians do not support it.
Fair trial: Christians agree → trial by jury (citizens decide guilt) is seen as good because evidence is fully heard, so the accused is judged fairly.

front: What is the death penalty, and what does the Bible say about it?
p1: Capital punishment: a state kills someone for a very serious crime → methods include hanging, lethal injection, firing squad and stoning.
p2: Support: 'Whoever sheds human blood, by humans shall their blood be shed' (Genesis); a fatal blow is punished by death (Exodus) → seen as fair.
p3: Against: 'do not resist an evil person' and 'love your enemies' (Matthew 5); Jesus saved the woman from stoning (John 8) → mercy and a chance to change.
s: Capital punishment: a state kills someone for a very serious crime → methods include hanging, lethal injection, firing squad and stoning.
Support: 'Whoever sheds human blood, by humans shall their blood be shed' (Genesis); a fatal blow is punished by death (Exodus) → seen as fair.
Against: 'do not resist an evil person' and 'love your enemies' (Matthew 5); Jesus saved the woman from stoning (John 8) → mercy and a chance to change.

front: What do non-religious people and situation ethicists think about the death penalty?
p1: For: it protects others from the criminal, people who take a life deserve to lose theirs, and it is a deterrent.
p2: Against: some executed people were later found innocent, two wrongs do not make a right, and countries with it do not have lower crime rates; Amnesty International campaigns against it.
p3: Situation ethics: ask what is most loving → some think execution is loving to victims and society; others think rehabilitation is always more loving.
s: For: it protects others from the criminal, people who take a life deserve to lose theirs, and it is a deterrent.
Against: some executed people were later found innocent, two wrongs do not make a right, and countries with it do not have lower crime rates; Amnesty International campaigns against it.
Situation ethics: ask what is most loving → some think execution is loving to victims and society; others think rehabilitation is always more loving.

front: What do Christians think about torture?
p1: Torture: harming someone to punish them or get information → most Christians are against it; it goes against human rights and Christian teachings of love and support.
p2: Situation ethics might allow it if it is the most loving act overall → for example, if someone planted a bomb and would not say where.
p3: Many Christians reject this → they say love for all people, including criminals, rules out torture.
s: Torture: harming someone to punish them or get information → most Christians are against it; it goes against human rights and Christian teachings of love and support.
Situation ethics might allow it if it is the most loving act overall → for example, if someone planted a bomb and would not say where.
Many Christians reject this → they say love for all people, including criminals, rules out torture.

front: What is Christian worship, and what are the types?
p1: Worship: Christians show respect and devotion to God → liturgical worship follows a script of set words and actions, often from a service book.
p2: Non-liturgical worship has no script → services still include prayers, music, Bible readings and a sermon, but the words are open; especially linked with Pentecostal churches.
p3: Personal worship: free worship alone → prayer, singing and Bible reading, to feel closer to God, give thanks or ask for something.
s: Worship: Christians show respect and devotion to God → liturgical worship follows a script of set words and actions, often from a service book.
Non-liturgical worship has no script → services still include prayers, music, Bible readings and a sermon, but the words are open; especially linked with Pentecostal churches.
Personal worship: free worship alone → prayer, singing and Bible reading, to feel closer to God, give thanks or ask for something.

front: What is the Book of Common Prayer, and why do Christians prefer different worship?
p1: Book of Common Prayer: oldest Church of England service book (16th century) → prayers and services for baptisms, weddings and funerals, plus the creeds and the 39 Articles.
p2: Some prefer liturgical worship → comfort and familiarity, clear order, deep tradition and confidence that the words are right and proper.
p3: Some prefer non-liturgical worship → openness to following the Holy Spirit, freedom to express worship (such as dancing) and flexibility for the congregation.
s: Book of Common Prayer: oldest Church of England service book (16th century) → prayers and services for baptisms, weddings and funerals, plus the creeds and the 39 Articles.
Some prefer liturgical worship → comfort and familiarity, clear order, deep tradition and confidence that the words are right and proper.
Some prefer non-liturgical worship → openness to following the Holy Spirit, freedom to express worship (such as dancing) and flexibility for the congregation.

front: What is a sacrament, and how many are there?
p1: Sacrament: an important Christian ceremony with a physical side (actions, sights, tastes) and a spiritual side, God's love or blessing → Roman Catholics believe God changes the spiritual world during it.
p2: Church of England: two sacraments (baptism and Eucharist), stated in Article 25 of the 39 Articles → they are signs of God's love.
p3: Roman Catholic and Orthodox Churches: seven sacraments → the difference is which ceremonies each Church thinks Jesus showed in the Bible.
s: Sacrament: an important Christian ceremony with a physical side (actions, sights, tastes) and a spiritual side, God's love or blessing → Roman Catholics believe God changes the spiritual world during it.
Church of England: two sacraments (baptism and Eucharist), stated in Article 25 of the 39 Articles → they are signs of God's love.
Roman Catholic and Orthodox Churches: seven sacraments → the difference is which ceremonies each Church thinks Jesus showed in the Bible.

front: What happens at baptism, and why is it important?
p1: Baptism: the ceremony that makes someone part of the Church, commanded by Jesus (Matthew 28) → in infant baptism a priest pours water on the head three times, for the Trinity and to wash away sins.
p2: Parents and godparents state their faith and hold a candle → this symbolises moving from sin to the light of Jesus.
p3: Baptist churches do not baptise infants → baptism should be chosen when old enough.
s: Baptism: the ceremony that makes someone part of the Church, commanded by Jesus (Matthew 28) → in infant baptism a priest pours water on the head three times, for the Trinity and to wash away sins.
Parents and godparents state their faith and hold a candle → this symbolises moving from sin to the light of Jesus.
Baptist churches do not baptise infants → baptism should be chosen when old enough.

front: What happens at the Eucharist, and what do Christians believe about it?
p1: Eucharist: re-enacts the Last Supper where Jesus spoke of the bread and wine as his body and blood → called Mass (Catholic) and Holy Communion (Church of England).
p2: Roman Catholics: the bread and wine literally become the body and blood of Christ → known as transubstantiation.
p3: Church of England: the bread and wine remind them of the death of Jesus and it saving them → the Salvation Army has no Eucharist at all.
s: Eucharist: re-enacts the Last Supper where Jesus spoke of the bread and wine as his body and blood → called Mass (Catholic) and Holy Communion (Church of England).
Roman Catholics: the bread and wine literally become the body and blood of Christ → known as transubstantiation.
Church of England: the bread and wine remind them of the death of Jesus and it saving them → the Salvation Army has no Eucharist at all.

front: What are the other Catholic and Orthodox sacraments?
p1: Confirmation: a bishop lays on hands as someone confirms their baptism → they choose to be a Christian. Holy orders: makes someone a priest.
p2: Marriage: a man and woman promise to God to love each other until death → Reconciliation: confessing sins to a priest, being truly sorry and doing penance.
p3: Anointing the sick: elders pray over the ill and anoint them with oil (James 5) → the priest lays on hands, seeking God's forgiveness and healing.
s: Confirmation: a bishop lays on hands as someone confirms their baptism → they choose to be a Christian. Holy orders: makes someone a priest.
Marriage: a man and woman promise to God to love each other until death → Reconciliation: confessing sins to a priest, being truly sorry and doing penance.
Anointing the sick: elders pray over the ill and anoint them with oil (James 5) → the priest lays on hands, seeking God's forgiveness and healing.

front: What is prayer, and what are the five types?
p1: Prayer: communicating with God → thanksgiving thanks God; contrition asks God for forgiveness.
p2: Supplication asks God for something → intercession asks God to help others.
p3: Worship offers praise and respect to God → prayers can be in public services or alone, scripted or freely invented.
s: Prayer: communicating with God → thanksgiving thanks God; contrition asks God for forgiveness.
Supplication asks God for something → intercession asks God to help others.
Worship offers praise and respect to God → prayers can be in public services or alone, scripted or freely invented.

front: What are set and informal prayer, and what do Christians think of them?
p1: Set prayers follow a script (such as the Book of Common Prayer) → liked for familiarity, long history, words checked by the Church, and feeling part of a community.
p2: Informal prayers do not follow a script → liked for freedom and spontaneity; often used in Pentecostal churches and seen as guided by the Holy Spirit.
p3: Most Christians use both → and nearly all use the Lord's Prayer.
s: Set prayers follow a script (such as the Book of Common Prayer) → liked for familiarity, long history, words checked by the Church, and feeling part of a community.
Informal prayers do not follow a script → liked for freedom and spontaneity; often used in Pentecostal churches and seen as guided by the Holy Spirit.
Most Christians use both → and nearly all use the Lord's Prayer.

front: What is the Lord's Prayer and what does it show?
p1: Jesus taught it to his followers (Matthew 6) → used by Christians around the world in church services and alone.
p2: 'Hallowed be your name' says God is holy → 'your kingdom come' asks that the world become God's kingdom; 'daily bread' asks for what Christians need to live.
p3: 'Forgive us' asks for forgiveness, and Christians promise to forgive others → it includes worship, contrition and supplication.
s: Jesus taught it to his followers (Matthew 6) → used by Christians around the world in church services and alone.
'Hallowed be your name' says God is holy → 'your kingdom come' asks that the world become God's kingdom; 'daily bread' asks for what Christians need to live.
'Forgive us' asks for forgiveness, and Christians promise to forgive others → it includes worship, contrition and supplication.

front: What is pilgrimage, and do all Christians think it matters?
p1: Pilgrimage: a special journey to a place important in the religion, started in the fourth century → to feel closer to God, ask for forgiveness or seek healing.
p2: Roman Catholic Church supports pilgrimage in its Catechism → for many Protestants it is important too, but they may go to different places.
p3: Some Protestants think pilgrimage is not vital → not wrong, but not essential; Jesus visited the Jerusalem temple aged twelve (Luke 2), so Christians may follow him.
s: Pilgrimage: a special journey to a place important in the religion, started in the fourth century → to feel closer to God, ask for forgiveness or seek healing.
Roman Catholic Church supports pilgrimage in its Catechism → for many Protestants it is important too, but they may go to different places.
Some Protestants think pilgrimage is not vital → not wrong, but not essential; Jesus visited the Jerusalem temple aged twelve (Luke 2), so Christians may follow him.

front: Why do Christians visit Jerusalem, Iona, Taize and Walsingham?
p1: Jerusalem: where Jesus died and was resurrected → pilgrims visit the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, the Mount of Olives and the Garden of Gethsemane.
p2: Iona: started by St Columba in 563 → pilgrims join worship and reflect on peace and social justice. Taize (France, 1940, Brother Roger): prayer, music and simple lives.
p3: Walsingham: in 1061 Lady Richeldis had a vision of Mary → a copy of the house of the Annunciation; Church of England, Catholic and Orthodox shrines.
s: Jerusalem: where Jesus died and was resurrected → pilgrims visit the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, the Mount of Olives and the Garden of Gethsemane.
Iona: started by St Columba in 563 → pilgrims join worship and reflect on peace and social justice. Taize (France, 1940, Brother Roger): prayer, music and simple lives.
Walsingham: in 1061 Lady Richeldis had a vision of Mary → a copy of the house of the Annunciation; Church of England, Catholic and Orthodox shrines.

front: What do Advent and Christmas remember?
p1: Advent: the start of the Christian year, preparing for Christmas → an advent wreath with four candles is lit on the four Sundays before Christmas, for Jesus the light of the world.
p2: Christmas (25th December): the birth of Jesus as told in Luke and Matthew → services include carols, vigils, midnight mass and nativity plays.
p3: Christmastide has 12 nights → ending on 6th January with Epiphany, which remembers the wise men visiting Jesus.
s: Advent: the start of the Christian year, preparing for Christmas → an advent wreath with four candles is lit on the four Sundays before Christmas, for Jesus the light of the world.
Christmas (25th December): the birth of Jesus as told in Luke and Matthew → services include carols, vigils, midnight mass and nativity plays.
Christmastide has 12 nights → ending on 6th January with Epiphany, which remembers the wise men visiting Jesus.

front: What do Holy Week and Easter remember?
p1: Holy Week: the week before Easter → Palm Sunday remembers Jesus entering Jerusalem on a donkey; Maundy Thursday the washing of feet and the Last Supper; Good Friday his death on the cross.
p2: Easter Sunday celebrates the resurrection → Paul says that without it Christianity is pointless; it shows that Christians will be resurrected too.
p3: Celebrations: palm crosses, foot washing, solemn processions on Good Friday → Easter services, vigils, and worship and praise of Jesus.
s: Holy Week: the week before Easter → Palm Sunday remembers Jesus entering Jerusalem on a donkey; Maundy Thursday the washing of feet and the Last Supper; Good Friday his death on the cross.
Easter Sunday celebrates the resurrection → Paul says that without it Christianity is pointless; it shows that Christians will be resurrected too.
Celebrations: palm crosses, foot washing, solemn processions on Good Friday → Easter services, vigils, and worship and praise of Jesus.

front: What are missionary work and evangelism, and why are they important?
p1: Missionary: invites people to convert to Christianity; evangelism: speaking about the gospel → the Great Commission is Jesus' command to preach to all creation (Mark 16).
p2: Missionaries spread Jesus' teachings, set up churches, translate the Bible and help with hospitals, schools and clean water → St Paul was the most famous early one.
p3: Christians follow the Great Commission and bring new members to the Church → non-Christians say it spreads Western values and can exploit vulnerable people.
s: Missionary: invites people to convert to Christianity; evangelism: speaking about the gospel → the Great Commission is Jesus' command to preach to all creation (Mark 16).
Missionaries spread Jesus' teachings, set up churches, translate the Bible and help with hospitals, schools and clean water → St Paul was the most famous early one.
Christians follow the Great Commission and bring new members to the Church → non-Christians say it spreads Western values and can exploit vulnerable people.

front: What is happening to the Church worldwide and in the UK?
p1: Christianity is the largest religion: around 2.5 billion followers → growth is largely down to missionaries.
p2: In the UK the Church is shrinking → a majority still say they are Christian, but only a small minority regularly go to church.
p3: Some UK churches are growing → 600 new Pentecostal churches have opened since 2010.
s: Christianity is the largest religion: around 2.5 billion followers → growth is largely down to missionaries.
In the UK the Church is shrinking → a majority still say they are Christian, but only a small minority regularly go to church.
Some UK churches are growing → 600 new Pentecostal churches have opened since 2010.

front: What does the local church do?
p1: A church is the community of Christians, not the building → St Paul calls it the Body of Christ, carrying on Jesus' actions on Earth; a parish is a local community of one denomination.
p2: Aims: preach the Bible, make God's kingdom real locally and support Christians → meetings, charity events, prayer for those in need, services and courses.
p3: 1 Peter tells elders to be shepherds, caring for the people → local churches may also work with other denominations (ecumenism).
s: A church is the community of Christians, not the building → St Paul calls it the Body of Christ, carrying on Jesus' actions on Earth; a parish is a local community of one denomination.
Aims: preach the Bible, make God's kingdom real locally and support Christians → meetings, charity events, prayer for those in need, services and courses.
1 Peter tells elders to be shepherds, caring for the people → local churches may also work with other denominations (ecumenism).

front: How does the worldwide Church work for reconciliation?
p1: Reconciliation: mending broken relationships → 'As I have loved you, so you must love one another'; the Church uses prayer, friendship, money and practical support.
p2: Ecumenism brings Christians of different denominations together → the World Council of Churches also works for peace through prayer, charity and campaigns.
p3: Persecution: treating people badly for their religion, politics or ethnicity → Christians face it in China, North Korea and India, and the Church supports them.

front: How do Christians show charity, and what does Christian Aid do?
p1: Jesus: 'love your neighbour as you love yourself' → Christians must give with love, not duty or to look good (1 Corinthians 13); some give in secret (Matthew 6).
p2: Ways to give: regular money, time and skills → some keep it secret, others publicise it to encourage others.
p3: Christian Aid: international charity → gives food, shelter and medical help in disasters, builds medical systems and clean water, and campaigns for justice.

Ways to give: regular money, time and skills → some keep it secret, others publicise it to encourage others.
Christian Aid: international charity → gives food, shelter and medical help in disasters, builds medical systems and clean water, and campaigns for justice.

front: What are ordinances, and what do the Articles say about the Eucharist?
p1: Ordinance: a symbolic act of obedience, not a means of receiving grace → the word some Protestant Churches use for the instructions given by Jesus.
p2: 39 Articles on the Eucharist: 'The Body of Christ is given, taken, and eaten in the Supper, only after a heavenly and spiritual manner' → a spiritual, not physical, meaning.
p3: The offering of Christ once made is the perfect redemption → so Christ's sacrifice is complete.

front: What do Christians believe about peace?
p1: Most Christians work towards a world without war → a peacemaker works for peace, and the sixth Commandment says 'do not kill'.
p2: Early Christians refused to fight in wars for many centuries → today some are pacifists, and others use only the violence needed to bring peace.
p3: Roman Catholic and Church of England teach war is sometimes needed → the lesser of two evils, to stop terrible evil.
s: Most Christians work towards a world without war → a peacemaker works for peace, and the sixth Commandment says 'do not kill'.
Early Christians refused to fight in wars for many centuries → today some are pacifists, and others use only the violence needed to bring peace.
Roman Catholic and Church of England teach war is sometimes needed → the lesser of two evils, to stop terrible evil.

front: How is Jesus a peacemaker, and what happened at his arrest?
p1: Jesus taught forgiveness, reconciliation and peace → at his arrest in Luke, a follower cuts off the servant's ear; Jesus says 'No more of this!' and heals it.
p2: Reading 1: all violence is wrong → Reading 2: personal violence is wrong, but not war between countries.
p3: Reading 3: only about that situation → Jesus needs to be arrested so he can die on the cross for everyone's sins.
s: Jesus taught forgiveness, reconciliation and peace → at his arrest in Luke, a follower cuts off the servant's ear; Jesus says 'No more of this!' and heals it.
Reading 1: all violence is wrong → Reading 2: personal violence is wrong, but not war between countries.
Reading 3: only about that situation → Jesus needs to be arrested so he can die on the cross for everyone's sins.

front: What do Christians teach about making peace?
p1: Sermon on the Mount: 'Blessed are the peacemakers' → and 'Love your enemies and pray for those who treat you badly'.
p2: Real peace needs justice (things being fair) → a Christian does not just avoid arguments by accepting unfairness.
p3: Second Vatican Council: peace cannot be achieved unless every person's well-being is safeguarded → Jesus taught forgiveness and reconciliation (mending broken relationships).
s: Sermon on the Mount: 'Blessed are the peacemakers' → and 'Love your enemies and pray for those who treat you badly'.
Real peace needs justice (things being fair) → a Christian does not just avoid arguments by accepting unfairness.
Second Vatican Council: peace cannot be achieved unless every person's well-being is safeguarded → Jesus taught forgiveness and reconciliation (mending broken relationships).

front: How do Christian groups work for peace?
p1: Four ways: holding talks, speaking out against brutal governments, informing people about injustice and non-violent protest.
p2: World Council of Churches: brings together Christians from around the world → arranges talks between people in arguments, to reconcile them.
p3: Pax Christi: international Roman Catholic group against all war → campaigns for talks and a fairer world.
s: Four ways: holding talks, speaking out against brutal governments, informing people about injustice and non-violent protest.
World Council of Churches: brings together Christians from around the world → arranges talks between people in arguments, to reconcile them.
Pax Christi: international Roman Catholic group against all war → campaigns for talks and a fairer world.

front: What causes conflict, and how do Christians respond?
p1: War: armed conflict between countries or large groups → causes include self-defence or fear, resources like oil, national pride, racism, politics and religion.
p2: Three Christian responses: talk (pacifists), fight (some wars are the lesser of two evils) → or campaign against causes of war such as injustice.
p3: All Christians agree on campaigning against injustice → because it is one of the causes of war.
s: War: armed conflict between countries or large groups → causes include self-defence or fear, resources like oil, national pride, racism, politics and religion.
Three Christian responses: talk (pacifists), fight (some wars are the lesser of two evils) → or campaign against causes of war such as injustice.
All Christians agree on campaigning against injustice → because it is one of the causes of war.

front: What does Matthew 26 say about conflict, and what is situation ethics?
p1: Jesus tells a follower: 'He who lives by the sword will die by the sword' → read as against all violence, against that one act, or only against personal violence.
p2: Situation ethics: do the most loving thing in each situation, not follow rules → violence could be most loving, such as war against Hitler.
p3: Many Christians reject it → they prefer set rules from the Bible and Church, and say the most loving act cannot be worked out.
s: Jesus tells a follower: 'He who lives by the sword will die by the sword' → read as against all violence, against that one act, or only against personal violence.
Situation ethics: do the most loving thing in each situation, not follow rules → violence could be most loving, such as war against Hitler.

front: Do Humanists think religion causes war, and how do Christians reply?
p1: Humanists aim to do the least harm → usually avoiding violence, but some war may stop greater harm.
p2: Some atheists say religion is a cause of war → examples are the Crusades, Protestant and Catholic conflict (30 Years War), and Kashmir.
p3: Christians reply: wars called religious are often about national identity → Christianity teaches God wants peace, and fighters misunderstand teachings.
s: Humanists aim to do the least harm → usually avoiding violence, but some war may stop greater harm.
Some atheists say religion is a cause of war → examples are the Crusades, Protestant and Catholic conflict (30 Years War), and Kashmir.

front: What is pacifism, and why are some Christians not pacifists?
p1: Pacifism: war and violence are always wrong → supported by 'You shall not murder', 'Love your enemies' and 'He who lives by the sword'.
p2: Quakers were one of the first pacifist Christian groups → in 1660 they committed never to fight or be in an army.
p3: Not pacifists: aggressors would have nothing to stop them, so evil could win → the Church of England supports Just Wars, and the Catholic Catechism allows lawful self-defence.
s: Pacifism: war and violence are always wrong → supported by 'You shall not murder', 'Love your enemies' and 'He who lives by the sword'.
Quakers were one of the first pacifist Christian groups → in 1660 they committed never to fight or be in an army.

front: What is passive resistance, and who used it?
p1: Passive resistance: working against something wrong without violence → it can include marches, petitions and breaking unfair laws.
p2: Jesus resisted without violence → he taught 'turn the other cheek' and love for enemies; in John he says 'the prince of this world is coming' and allows his arrest.
p3: Martin Luther King Jr. used protests, marches and boycotts for equal rights in the 1950s and 60s → he told followers not to use violence.

front: What are the conditions of a Just War?
p1: Just War theory: a war should be fought only for good reason and in the right way → a good reason such as self-defence or ending injustice.
p2: Started by the government, backed by the United Nations → the last resort, with a good chance of winning, fought to bring peace.
p3: Civilians must not be targeted → methods should be enough to win but no more, keeping suffering to a minimum.
s: Just War theory: a war should be fought only for good reason and in the right way → a good reason such as self-defence or ending injustice.

front: How does the Bible support Just War, and what are the problems?
p1: Bible support: God trains hands for war (Psalm 144); obey governments (Romans 13); buy a sword (Luke 22); laying down your life for a friend (John 15).
p2: Problems: pacifists say no war can be just → war is hard to limit once started, and both sides think God is on theirs.
p3: Situation ethics supports a war if it is the most loving thing → but may disagree about which wars.
s: Bible support: God trains hands for war (Psalm 144); obey governments (Romans 13); buy a sword (Luke 22); laying down your life for a friend (John 15).

front: What is Holy War, and what does the Bible say?
p1: Holy war: a war seen as supported by God → to spread or defend a religion, take revenge or take back holy places; ordered by a religious leader, with Heaven promised.
p2: Old Testament examples: God commands Joshua to attack Jericho → in the New Testament Jesus says 'I did not come to bring peace, but a sword'.
p3: Many Christians read the 'sword' as metaphorical → the struggle against evil within people and in the world.

p1: Pacifists and Just War supporters reject Holy War → God would not command or take sides in war; Pope John Paul II said the Crusades (1091-1295) did not follow Jesus' teachings.
p2: Atheists and Humanists oppose it → no God to order it, it goes against free choice of religion, and a loving God would not order suffering.
p3: Christians may agree → God is used as an excuse; some speak of a spiritual war against evil and injustice.

front: What are WMD, and why do Christians disagree about them?
p1: WMD cause huge damage and kill thousands → nuclear, biological (bacteria and viruses) and chemical (poisons such as mustard gas).
p2: Against: difficult to control, huge destruction against pacifism and Just War, harm to civilians and the environment.
p3: For: possession deters attack, so keeps peace → a country with them can wipe out any attacker.

front: What do the Churches and the Bible say about WMD?
p1: Roman Catholic Church: WMD are wrong, killing civilians → Pope Benedict XVI: 'In a nuclear war there would be no victors, only victims'.
p2: Church of England: nuclear weapons are needed for defence, but using them would never be right → in 2010 it accepted a duty to deter nuclear aggression.
p3: Deuteronomy 20: God commands Israelites to destroy nations → some say it did not come from God; a few justify WMD with it; most call it ancient.

front: What do utilitarians and situation ethicists, and Humanists, think about WMD?
p1: Utilitarianism: bring about the greatest good for the greatest number → against: war could harm everyone and WMD cost billions; for: they deter attacks.

p3: Humanists differ: some are pacifists, others think WMD are needed → Joseph Fletcher supported the bombing of Japan.

front: Which Qur'an quotes show that Allah is one?

front: Which Qur'an quotes show how believers should live together?

p1: Qur'an: “it is meant for those in need: the poor, those who collect it, those in debt, new Muslims.” This charity goes to named groups.

front: Which Qur'an quotes show when fighting is allowed?

front: Which quotes show why Id-ul-Ghadeer matters to Shi'a Muslims?
p1: Qur'an: “Today, I have perfected your religion for you, completed My favour upon you, and chosen Islam as your way of life.” This verse is linked to the day Ali was announced as leader.

front: Which quotes show how Allah created the universe?

Qur'an: “It is Allah who created day and night, the sun and the moon, each moving in its own path.” This shows order in creation.

front: Which quotes show how Allah makes human life?
p1: Qur'an: “He created humans from clay and then from a drop of fluid.” Humans have a physical beginning.

p3: Hadith: “After that, Allah sends an angel to record four things: your deeds, your lifespan, your provision.” Then the soul is breathed in.
s: Qur'an: “He created humans from clay and then from a drop of fluid.” Humans have a physical beginning.

front: Which Qur'an quotes show that life is sacred?
p1: Qur'an: “If anyone kills a person unjustly, it is as if they have killed all of humanity.” Every life is equally valuable.

s: Qur'an: “If anyone kills a person unjustly, it is as if they have killed all of humanity.” Every life is equally valuable.

front: Which Qur'an quotes show that life is a test?

s: Qur'an: “He created life and death to test who does good deeds.” This life is a test of behaviour.
Qur'an: “We will surely test you with fear, hunger, loss of wealth, lives, and crops.” Suffering is met with patience.
Qur'an: “We belong to Allah, and to Him we will return.” Muslims say this in hardship to show trust in Allah.

front: Which Qur'an quotes show the Hereafter and judgement?
p1: Qur'an: “Everything you have in this world is temporary, but what is with Allah lasts forever.” The afterlife matters more than wealth and power.

s: Qur'an: “Everything you have in this world is temporary, but what is with Allah lasts forever.” The afterlife matters more than wealth and power.
Qur'an: “every soul will be judged for what it has done, and no one will be wronged.” This judgement is fair.

front: Which quotes show Muslim teaching on food and animals?
p1: Hadith: “The Prophet (PBUH) ate meat, and he said it is the best food for strength.” Eating meat is allowed.

s: Hadith: “The Prophet (PBUH) ate meat, and he said it is the best food for strength.” Eating meat is allowed.

front: Which Bible quotes show the Holy Spirit's role in creation?

s: Bible: “the Spirit of God was hovering over the waters.” The Holy Spirit is present at creation.

front: Which Bible quotes show who Jesus is?
p1: Bible: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” Jesus is the Word, who is God.

s: Bible: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” Jesus is the Word, who is God.
Bible: “He appeared in the flesh, was vindicated by the Spirit, was seen by angels.” This describes the incarnation.

front: Which quotes show Christian beliefs about judgement and eternal life?
p1: Bible: “Then they will go away to eternal punishment, but the righteous to eternal life.” People are separated at judgement.
p2: Bible: “we have a building from God, an eternal house in heaven, not built by human hands.” Heaven is the Christian's true home.

s: Bible: “Then they will go away to eternal punishment, but the righteous to eternal life.” People are separated at judgement.
Bible: “we have a building from God, an eternal house in heaven, not built by human hands.” Heaven is the Christian's true home.
Church teaching: “Christ will return to judge all people on the last day.” This is the Final Judgement.

front: Which quotes show the disagreement about Purgatory?
p1: Church teaching: “The idea of Purgatory is an invention that has no proof in the Bible.” The Church of England rejects it.

s: Church teaching: “The idea of Purgatory is an invention that has no proof in the Bible.” The Church of England rejects it.

Bible: “It is a good and holy thing to pray for the dead so that they may be freed from sin.” Catholics use this to support prayers for the dead.

front: Which quotes from Job show how Christians respond to suffering?

s: Bible: “Job was blameless and upright; he feared God and shunned evil.” Job suffered although he was good.

front: Which Psalm quotes give comfort in suffering?
p1: Bible: “Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light on my path.” God's word guides believers.
p2: Bible: “My comfort in my suffering is this: Your promise preserves my life.” God's promise brings hope.

s: Bible: “Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light on my path.” God's word guides believers.
Bible: “My comfort in my suffering is this: Your promise preserves my life.” God's promise brings hope.

Bible: “You rulers of Israel, you hate justice and twist what is right.” Micah warns leaders who are unfair.

front: Which Bible quotes show that Christians must speak up for the vulnerable?

Bible: “Speak up for those who cannot speak for themselves, for the rights of all who are destitute.” Christians give a voice to the voiceless.

front: Which Bible quotes show how Christians should treat people who sin?
p1: Bible: “Let any one of you who is without sin be the first to throw a stone at her.” Nobody is perfect, so nobody should judge harshly.
